summary: The Gurjara-Pratiharas rose in Rajasthan and Malwa around 730, winning fame for holding back the Arab armies of Sind. After decades of war with the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan over Kannauj, Nagabhata II took the city, and under Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala I (836–910) the empire ruled most of the northern plains. Rashtrakuta raids, breakaway vassals and Mahmud of Ghazni's sack of Kannauj in 1018 reduced it to a small kingdom that ended around 1036.
details: In the 720s and 730s the Umayyad governors of Sind sent armies into Rajasthan and Gujarat. The Pratihara dynasty, which probably began in the Jalore–Bhinmal area and spread to Ujjain, emerged as a leader of the resistance under its founder Nagabhata I. Many historians believe he repulsed the Arabs near Ujjain, though where he fought them is uncertain; in 738–39 a Chalukya army decisively beat them at Navsari in Gujarat. By 743 the Arabs had lost their conquests in Rajasthan and Gujarat, and the Pratiharas had a firm base in western India.

Kannauj, the old capital of Harsha, was the prize of northern India, and three powers fought for it: the Pratiharas, the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan. Around 785–790 the Pratihara king Vatsaraja forced the ruler of Kannauj to accept his overlordship and sent an army that defeated the Pala king Dharmapala. But the Rashtrakuta king Dhruva crossed the Narmada and defeated Vatsaraja, then Dharmapala too, before going home in 790. This 'tripartite struggle' would last for a generation.

Vatsaraja's son Nagabhata II faced another Rashtrakuta invasion. Around 798–800 the Rashtrakuta king Govinda III marched north, defeated Nagabhata near Gwalior and conquered Malwa and other lands. The ruler of Kannauj, Chakrayudha, surrendered, and Dharmapala of Bengal also submitted. Like his father, Govinda soon returned to the Deccan, but the Pratiharas lost Malwa and Gujarat for a time. Nagabhata later recovered Malwa, and the Rashtrakuta threat ended when Govinda died in 814.

Freed from Rashtrakuta pressure, Nagabhata II invaded the Ganges–Yamuna Doab, defeated Chakrayudha, the Pala-backed king of Kannauj, and took the city. He then fought Dharmapala himself near Munger, in Bihar, and won a decisive victory. One account dates this to 816, but a Rashtrakuta inscription from Baroda dated 812 already records his victory over the Pala king. The Pratiharas had won the long struggle: Kannauj became their capital for two centuries.

Mihira Bhoja, who followed the short reign of Ramabhadra, ruled from Kannauj from about 836 to 885 and took the title Adivaraha, which appears on his coins. Between 833 and 842 Pratihara forces drove the Arabs out of Kutch. After the death of the Pala king Devapala, Bhoja defeated his successor Narayanapala and pushed east. At its height his empire reached the Narmada in the south, the Sutlej in the northwest and the edge of Bengal in the east, making it the greatest power in northern India.

Arab merchants and geographers who traded with India wrote about its kingdoms. The account attributed to Sulaiman, written around 851, described the 'Gurjara' king, meaning the Pratihara emperor: 'The ruler of Gurjara maintains numerous forces and no other Indian prince has so fine a cavalry.' The same account described the Pala kingdom of Bengal, which it called Ruhmi. The description fits Mihira Bhoja's reign, when Pratihara armies guarded the western frontier against the Arab states of Sind and fought rivals to the east and south.

The Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas still competed for Gujarat and Malwa. Mihira Bhoja intervened in a succession struggle among the Rashtrakutas' Gujarat branch; his cavalry raid was repulsed, but he kept parts of Gujarat and Malwa. Around 880, or at least before 888, the Rashtrakuta king Krishna II defeated the Pratiharas at Ujjain, the main city of Malwa. The setback did not last: by the end of his reign Bhoja had ended the Gujarat Rashtrakuta line, and the empire's southwestern frontier held.

Mihira Bhoja is thought to have died around 885, and his son Mahendrapala I ruled until about 910. He kept his father's empire intact and pushed its frontiers further east; the historian R. C. Majumdar describes it as stretching from the Himalayas to the Vindhya range. An unclear verse in the Kashmiri chronicle Rajatarangini hints that he may have lost some land in the Punjab to Kashmir. His teacher, the poet Rajashekhara, called him the great king of Aryavarta and celebrated the splendour of Kannauj.

After Mahendrapala's death the Pratihara royal family quarrelled over the throne. The Rashtrakuta king Indra III, crowned in 915, took advantage. He marched north into the Ganges–Yamuna Doab and attacked Kannauj, while his vassal chased the Pratihara emperor Mahipala I, who, a Kannada poet wrote, 'fled as if struck by lightning'. Kannauj was badly damaged and held by the Rashtrakutas until about 916. The Pratiharas soon regained their capital, but the blow to their prestige was lasting.

Mahipala I still claimed a wide empire, but after him a series of short reigns weakened the dynasty. Its vassal families, once loyal governors and allies, began to act as independent kings: the Paramaras in Malwa, the Chandelas in Bundelkhand, the Kalachuris, the Tomaras around Delhi and the Chahamanas in Rajasthan. Around 950 the Chandelas seized the great fortress of Gwalior. By the late 10th century the Pratiharas held little more than the region around Kannauj.

Mahmud of Ghazni, ruler of a Turkic empire based in Afghanistan, led repeated raids into northern India in search of plunder. In 1018 he marched on Kannauj. The Pratihara king Rajyapala abandoned the city and fled, and Mahmud captured it. The Chandela king Vidyadhara later had Rajyapala killed and placed Trilochanapala on the Pratihara throne as his puppet. The once-imperial dynasty, which had ruled the northern plains a century earlier, now depended on the favour of its own former vassals.

After Trilochanapala, the last known ruler of the dynasty was Yasahpala, who reigned from about 1024 until his death in 1036. By then the Pratiharas held only a small territory around Kannauj and lived in the shadow of the Chandelas and other former vassals. With Yasahpala the line that had defended the west against the Arabs and ruled Kannauj for two centuries disappears from the records. Its lands passed to the regional kingdoms that had grown out of its former provinces.
